title: Why a Crucified Messiah? The Scandal of the Cross

keyTerms.d: Crucifixion was regarded as the most degrading form of execution, inflicted above all on slaves and rebels — the servile supplicium. Josephus called it “the most wretched of deaths”; it was deliberately public and deliberately obscene.

“A hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), a text applied to crucifixion in Second Temple Judaism and by Paul in Galatians 3:13. A crucified body hanging on a Roman cross was, on the face of the text, a body under the visible curse of God — so “crucified Messiah” was very nearly a contradiction in terms.

The claim is narrower and firmer than “no Jew ever imagined a suffering figure”: the dominant hope was for a triumphant deliverer, and a crucified Messiah — executed as a criminal, hung under the Deuteronomic curse, by Rome — was the opposite of what that hope expected and, to most first-century Jews, an offense to be resisted rather than a promise to be welcomed.

The crucifixion’s bedrock status rests first on plain attestation: it is reported not only by Christians but by non-Christian writers with no motive to flatter the movement — the Roman historian Tacitus, and (in a notice whose core is widely accepted as authentic) Josephus — and even determinedly skeptical scholars grant it.

The reasoning that a tradition so damaging to its own cause is unlikely to have been invented. It is a tool of probability, not proof, and has itself been criticized as unreliable when used alone — which is why the crucifixion’s certainty is anchored on the attestation, not on the criterion by itself.

Strictly, the point is not that the crucifixion embarrassed the Christians who preached it — they gloried in it — but that no one setting out to invent a Messiah, and no audience they hoped to win, would ever have chosen this detail. Here it does not stand alone but reinforces the attestation.

Galatians 3:13: the exact verse (Deuteronomy 21:23) that made a crucified Messiah a scandal becomes the key to what the crucifixion accomplished. The curse was real, and it was borne, willingly, in the place of those who deserved it. It never means that the Father hated or was divided from the Son, nor that the divine nature could die or be cursed.

How exactly the cross saves — the mechanism of the atonement — is a question on which sincere Christians have long differed: penalty borne, victory over the powers, satisfaction, recapitulation, self-giving love. These are the family’s internal debate, held within a shared confession: “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and in that death the curse was borne and God and sinners reconciled.

derive.q: The death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels, on a body the Law called “cursed by God” — so “crucified Messiah” was…?
derive.ans: very nearly a contradiction in terms
derive.why: The Messiah was the LORD’s anointed, the son of David who would break the nations and reign — not a condemned criminal dying under God’s own curse at the hands of the pagan empire he was supposed to overthrow. A crucified Messiah looked less like a vindicated king than like a blasphemous joke.

derive.q: Inventors do not sabotage their own inventions — yet the earliest Christians put the most damaging detail at the dead center of their preaching. So that is…?
derive.why: A group fabricating a messianic hero from scratch, or gilding the memory of a beloved teacher, has every reason to leave out the detail that most discredits the claim — and crucifixion was that detail. Placing the offense at the center is what looks like a community stuck with a fact it could not deny and did not choose.

derive.q: They were not embarrassed by the cross — they gloried in it. So, strictly, the argument’s point is…?
derive.ans: not their embarrassment, but that no inventor would choose it
derive.why: Strictly, the point is not that the crucifixion embarrassed the Christians who preached it, but that no one setting out to invent a Messiah, and no audience they hoped to win, would ever have chosen this detail; a claim so damaging to its own cause is not the kind a movement fabricates.

derive.q: The no-one-would-invent-it reasoning is a probability tool with real critics. So the crucifixion’s certainty rests on…?
derive.ans: the attestation first — the criterion only reinforces it
derive.why: Its bedrock status rests first on plain attestation, including non-Christian writers with no motive to flatter the movement. The criterion has been criticized as unreliable when used alone, which is why the certainty is anchored on the attestation, not on the criterion by itself.

derive.q: In first-century categories, a resurrection marks a vindicated martyr, and nothing in the sources treats rising as the sign of the Messiah. So the title “Messiah” was…?
derive.ans: very hard to derive from Easter alone — something like it was already attached
derive.why: When popular talk held that John the Baptist had risen, no one concluded the risen John was the Christ. The apostles read the resurrection as God’s confirmation of the title, but a confirmation needs something to confirm: something like the claim was already attached to Jesus before he died, at least in the charge Rome wrote over his cross.

derive.q: Grant all of it: the crucifixion is bedrock, and the first Christians centered it. Does that, by itself, prove Jesus rose?
derive.why: The offensiveness of the cross explains why no one would fabricate it; it does not explain why anyone would then celebrate it. For that a further event is needed — the vindication the first Christians claimed had occurred, argued on its own evidence. The scandal clears the ground; it does not, alone, raise the dead.

honestState.p1: The crucifixion is, by wide agreement, the most secure single fact about Jesus of Nazareth. Its bedrock status rests first on plain attestation — Christian and non-Christian (Tacitus, and the widely accepted core of Josephus) — and even determinedly skeptical scholars grant it. The scandal adds a second, converging consideration: a claim so damaging to its own cause is not the kind a movement fabricates.
honestState.fairness: Two cautions are owed. The point about Jewish expectation is easily overstated: some read the Servant of Isaiah 53 in an individual, even messianic key (the Targum on Isaiah 52:13 names “my servant the Messiah,” even though it redirects the Servant’s sufferings to Israel and the nations), and later tradition knew of a suffering “Messiah son of Joseph” — the claim is only that the dominant hope was triumphant. And the un-invention reasoning is a historian’s tool of probability, not a proof; it has been criticized as unreliable when used alone, which is why it reinforces the attestation rather than replacing it.
honestState.verdict: The scandal of the cross is powerful evidence that the crucifixion is historical bedrock — the kind of fact a movement is stuck with, not the kind it invents — and that the earliest Christians met it not with denial but with a developed theology of the curse borne. It does not, on its own, demonstrate that the theology is true, nor that Jesus rose; those rest on further evidence. And we say it with the first Christians: the crucified Jesus is the Messiah; his death was for our sins, the curse borne and God and sinners reconciled; and God raised him. The scandal does not prove that last claim, but it clears the ground for it.

order: A crucified Messiah was the single most offensive claim in its world.
The crucifixion is therefore historical bedrock — multiply attested, and not a detail anyone inventing a Messiah would choose.
Therefore the crucifixion is authentic bedrock, and the New Testament answers the scandal rather than evading it.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and how narrow the claim is.
cards.a: A crucified Messiah was the single most offensive claim in its world. The claim is narrow and firm: not that no strand of ancient Judaism ever contemplated a suffering righteous figure, but that the dominant hope was for a triumphant deliverer, and a crucified Messiah — executed as a criminal, hung under the Deuteronomic curse, by Rome — was the opposite of what that hope expected.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what it rests on first.
cards.a: The crucifixion is historical bedrock. It rests first on plain attestation — reported by non-Christian writers with no motive to flatter the movement, and granted even by determinedly skeptical scholars. Converging with that: no one inventing a Messiah, and no audience they hoped to win, would choose the detail most damaging to the claim.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the crucifixion is authentic bedrock, not fabrication, and that the earliest Christians met it with a theology of the curse borne. Not, by itself, that Jesus rose or that the theology is true. The offensiveness of the cross explains why no one would fabricate it; it does not explain why anyone would then celebrate it.

cards.q: Why was the cross so shameful to a Roman or a Greek?
cards.a: It was an instrument of torture so degrading that polite Romans avoided the word — the slaves’ punishment, reserved for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, deliberately public and deliberately obscene. The very word “cross” was to be kept far from a citizen’s body, thoughts, eyes, and ears. To announce that one worshipped a crucified man was, to a cultured Greek or Roman, simply folly.

cards.q: Why did the offense cut deeper for a Jew?
cards.a: Because it touched God directly. The Law said “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and a crucified body hanging on a Roman cross was, on the face of the text, a body under the visible curse of God — at the hands of the pagan empire the Messiah was supposed to overthrow.

cards.q: Why is the scandal of the cross evidence rather than a weakness?
cards.a: Inventors do not sabotage their own inventions. A group fabricating a messianic hero, or gilding the memory of a beloved teacher, has every reason to leave out the detail that most discredits the claim — and crucifixion was that detail. Placing it at the dead center of the preaching is what looks like a community stuck with a fact it could not deny and did not choose.

cards.q: Didn’t the first Christians manage the cross as an awkward fact?
cards.a: The reverse: they gloried in it. “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2); “far be it from me to boast except in the cross” (Galatians 6:14). The offense was not an awkwardness to be managed on the way to the message; it was the message.

cards.q: What makes the persecutor-turned-apostle the sharpest illustration?
cards.a: He found the crucified-Messiah claim so intolerable that he set out to destroy the people making it (Galatians 1:13–14); he of all people understood the Deuteronomic curse. That the movement’s most capable enemy became its most relentless missionary — and never once tried to soften the scandal he had once found damning — is a fact demanding explanation.

cards.q: How does the New Testament answer the curse — and what does it not mean?
cards.a: Through the offending text itself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23). The curse was real, and it was borne, willingly, in the place of those who deserved it — the scandal absorbed and turned inside out. It never means that the Father hated or was divided from the Son, nor that the divine nature could die or be cursed.

cards.q: Would the resurrection alone explain why they called Jesus the Messiah?
cards.a: Not on its own. In first-century categories a resurrection would mark someone out as a vindicated martyr; Jews who hoped for resurrection looked for the dead to be raised together at the end of the age, and nothing in our sources treats rising from the dead as the sign of the Messiah. Easter confirmed the title (Acts 2:36), but a confirmation needs something to confirm: something like the claim was already attached to Jesus before he died, at least in Rome’s charge over his cross.

cards.q: Does this case settle how the cross saves?
cards.a: No, deliberately. Some traditions emphasize Christ bearing the penalty of sin in our place; others, his victory over sin and death; others, satisfaction, recapitulation, or self-giving love. That is the family’s internal debate, held within a shared confession: “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and in that death the curse was borne and God and sinners reconciled.

cards.q: Reply to: “‘He became a curse for us’ makes God a divine child-abuser.”
cards.a: It targets one crude version of one theory of the atonement, not the shared confession — and misreads even that. On classical Christian teaching the one who “became a curse for us” is not a third party the Father abuses but God himself, the eternal Son, willingly giving himself: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). It never means the Father hated the Son, nor that the divine nature could die or be cursed.

obj.q: Dying-and-rising gods were everywhere — Osiris, Adonis, Baal. A crucified and vindicated savior is just an old pagan template in Jewish clothes; there is nothing un-inventable about it.
obj.model: This gets the evidence backwards. The simple “dying-and-rising god as source of Christianity” thesis is now widely abandoned — and even Tryggve Mettinger, who has maintained against the prevailing view that some such figures existed, found no prima facie evidence that the death and resurrection of Jesus is a mythological construct drawing on them. But the decisive point is narrower: no pagan template involved crucifixion, the Roman slaves’ death, or a savior under the curse of the Jewish Law. Those are the exact features that made the Christian claim offensive to Jew and Greek alike. A movement borrowing a flattering myth does not borrow the one detail that repels its whole audience.

obj.q: “They wouldn’t have invented a crucified Messiah” can look like a just-so story dressed as history. The criterion of embarrassment is easy to abuse, hard to falsify, and often assumes we know what an ancient author would or would not have found embarrassing.
obj.model: Grant what is true in it: that reasoning is a historian’s tool of probability, not a proof, and has been criticized as unreliable when used alone — and notice the argument does not rest on the criterion. The crucifixion’s bedrock status rests first on plain multiple attestation: it is reported by non-Christian writers with no motive to flatter the movement, and granted even by determined sceptics. The scandal is a converging consideration, offered as a probability, not a proof. Nor do we have to guess what the ancient audience found offensive: Paul says so himself — “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23). And it avoids the usual circularity charge: the point is not the vague “embarrassing to the tradents” — they gloried in the cross — but the sharper, more falsifiable claim that a detail this damaging to one’s own cause is not what a movement fabricates to win converts.

obj.q: Isaiah 53 describes a suffering servant, some ancient Jewish texts read it messianically, and later tradition knew of a suffering “Messiah son of Joseph.” So a suffering Messiah was a live category — the cross was no scandal.
obj.model: Keep the distinction. Ancient Judaism was not monolithic: the Servant of Isaiah 53 was read by some in an individual, even messianic key (the Targum on Isaiah 52:13 names “my servant the Messiah,” even though the Targum itself redirects the Servant’s sufferings to Israel and the nations), and later tradition knew of a suffering “Messiah son of Joseph.” The claim is narrower and firmer: the dominant hope was for a triumphant deliverer, and a crucified Messiah — executed as a criminal, hung under the Deuteronomic curse, by Rome — was the opposite of what that hope expected. The specific scandal was never “suffering” in the abstract; it was the Roman cross.

obj.q: Proclaiming the cross louder is cognitive dissonance at work: when reality contradicts a deeply held belief, people re-rationalize the failure and proclaim it harder than before.
obj.model: Dissonance theory describes a group preserving an existing belief despite disconfirmation. Dissonance reduction can explain a group doubling down on what it already hoped for. It is poorly suited to explain a group proclaiming a brand-new category — a crucified and cursed Messiah, raised bodily ahead of the last day — contrary to its entire tradition, to describe a man it had given up for lost.

unseen.q: Mark doesn’t center the shame — he dresses the execution up as a royal scene: purple robe, crown, acclamation, the title over the cross. Some scholars even hear a Roman triumphal procession in it. That’s spin, the very minimizing you say the first Christians never did.
unseen.model: Look at what the scene actually is. The soldiers dress Jesus in purple, press a crown of thorns onto his head, and salute him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” (Mark 15:17–18); the charge over the cross repeats the title (15:26). It is a mock coronation meant to humiliate, and Mark lets it stand, for his readers, as truth its mockers did not intend. The proposed triumphal-procession parallel is disputed, and nothing here depends on it; the mockery of the title itself is plain in the text. Mark’s posture is the same as Paul’s, and it is hard to explain as invention or salesmanship: people selling a fabricated hero do not stake everything on his most humiliating hour. People convinced that the most humiliating hour had been reversed — and had turned out to mean something — might.
